title: Hearing Dizzy Gillespie's first bebop band and reacting to bebop
summary: Stewart heard the 1944 band with Pettiford and Don Byas; he found Gillespie's playing a bit way out while Parker was more pleasant, and he did not explain it to others.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

Well now, that was -- from what I've read, that was apparently a very controversial band, first, because it was the first so called be-bop band. How did they strike you when you heard them?
Well, be-bop had just come in, and it sounded real good. Of course, not being into be-bop all that much, I, at times I kind of thought that it would -- it was a little bit too way out, you know.
In what respect?
The chords, I mean, went in and out and the riffs that -- that they would make -- individual players would make at times, playing a whole lot of notes that at
times didn't -- that to me didn't go over too well, with me, that is.

They'd see how fast they could play different riffs, you know, and what have you, when they could make it a little more simple and make it sound a little more pleasing, I think.

Did you -- did you find these characteristics to be -- you know, I sometimes felt that about Gillespie's playing, but I never -- and some other people, some other guys that came along, but I never really got that impression from Parker at all. Did you?
Not from Parker as much as Gillespie, like you say.
Because it seemed to me like Parker always, he was a melodic --
He was a little cool about it, you know, pleasant, a little more pleasant with it.
Well, yeah, he had a prettier sound too.
That's right.
Because Dizzy's sound could be kind of --
Oh, yeah.
-- I mean, if you compared it to like Louis Armstrong or somebody, he really had the sound, had that didn't
kind of body to it.
Right.

So sometimes -- that might be one of kind of abrasive. the reasons why some of those ideas came off (inaudible). But were you -- so that you, when you first -- when you first heard Pettiford and those guys playing, it sounded pretty good to you at that point?
Oh, yes, it did, sure.
Well, now -- but now, a lot of the players who had developed in the '30s didn't like him at all.
Yes, I know it.
But did you -- given the amount of knowledge that you -- harmonic knowledge that you had, were you able to explain to some of the other guys what they were playing?

Well, no, I didn't -- I didn't even take time to go into it, as far as the explanation of it was concerned. I just went on, played it with them and -- you know what I mean, in my way, and just more or less fell right in with it.
